name: C
description: C is a fast, low-level language that teaches how memory and programs really work.

blocks.html:
Introduction to C

What is C?

C is a small, fast programming language created by Dennis Ritchie in the early 1970s. Many things you use every day are written in C or built on it: operating systems, databases, and the software inside phones and cars. Other languages such as C++, Java and Python borrowed ideas from C, so learning C makes them easier later.

C is a compiled language. You write source code in a text file, and a program called the compiler turns it into a machine-code file that your computer can run. C is also close to the hardware. It lets you see how memory really works, and that is why it is a great teaching language.

Compile and run with gcc

GCC is a free compiler that works on Linux, macOS and Windows. Save your code in a file called hello.c, then type these commands in a terminal:

gcc hello.c -o hello
./hello

The first command compiles hello.c and writes a program named hello (the -o option sets the output name). The second command runs it. On Windows with MinGW the program is hello.exe and you run it with hello. If the compiler finds mistakes, it prints error messages with line numbers and does not create the program.

Your first program

blocks.output: Hello, Learning Hub!

blocks.html:
Let us read this program line by line.

  • #include <stdio.h> copies the standard input/output header into your file. It tells the compiler about printf.
  • int main(void) is the main function. Every C program starts running here.
  • printf("...") prints text on the screen. The \n inside the text means "start a new line".
  • return 0; tells the operating system the program finished without errors.
  • Each statement ends with a semicolon ; and a block of code is wrapped in curly braces { }.

Escape sequences and comments

Inside a string, a backslash starts a special code called an escape sequence. Comments are notes for humans. The compiler ignores them. Use /* ... */ for many lines and // ... for one line.

EscapeMeaning
\nnew line
\ttab
\"a double quote inside a string
\\one backslash

blocks.output:
Course: C Programming
She said "hello"
Folder: C:\temp
Line one
Line two

blocks.html: Now a program that does a small calculation. Notice that %d in the text is a placeholder that printf replaces with an integer value.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement.
  • Forgetting #include <stdio.h>, so printf is unknown.
  • Writing Printf or Main. C is case sensitive, so the names must be exact.
  • Forgetting \n, so the next prompt appears on the same line.

Key Points

  • C is a compiled language: source code (.c) is turned into a program by a compiler such as gcc.
  • gcc hello.c -o hello compiles, and ./hello runs the result.
  • Every program starts in main.
  • printf from stdio.h prints text; \n makes a new line.
  • Statements end with ; and C is case sensitive.

Variables, Types & Input/Output

Variables and basic types

A variable is a named box in memory that stores a value. In C you must tell the compiler the type of every variable before you use it. The type decides what kind of value fits in the box and how much memory it takes.

TypeStoresExample
intwhole numbersint age = 19;
floatdecimal numbers (about 6 digits of precision)float gpa = 3.5f;
doubledecimal numbers (about 15 digits of precision)double pi = 3.14159;
charone character, stored as a small numberchar grade = 'A';

Characters use single quotes ('A'). Strings use double quotes ("Hello") and you will meet them later. A variable that is not given a value holds garbage, so always set a starting value.

Printing with format specifiers

printf uses format specifiers that start with %. Each specifier is replaced by the next value in the list. The type of the value must match the specifier.

SpecifierUsed for
%dint
%ffloat or double (use %.2f for 2 decimals)
%cchar shown as a character
%sstring

blocks.output:
Age: 19
GPA: 3.5
Pi: 3.14
Grade: A
Grade as a number: 65
Width: [   42] [42   ]

blocks.html:
Notice that a char is really a small number. Printing it with %c shows the letter, and printing it with %d shows its code (65 for 'A' in ASCII). The number in %5d sets a minimum width, and - left-aligns the value.

Reading input with scanf

scanf reads values from the keyboard. It uses the same specifiers, but you must give the address of the variable with the & operator, so scanf knows where to store the value. For example:

int age;
scanf("%d", &age);   /* user types 19 and presses Enter */

For a double variable, scanf needs %lf (with a letter l). The demo below cannot wait for a keyboard, so it uses sscanf. It works exactly like scanf, but it reads from a string that is already in the program. Imagine the user typed 19 3.5 B.

blocks.output:
Read 3 values
Age=19 GPA=3.5 Grade=B

blocks.html:
Constants

When a value must never change, make it a constant. Use const before the type, or #define to give a name to a value before compiling. Names written in capital letters are a common habit for constants.

blocks.output:
Pass mark: 50
Total with tax: 230.00

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Forgetting & in scanf: scanf("%d", age) is wrong, it must be &age.
  • Using %d to print a double. The output will be wrong. Use %f.
  • Using a variable before giving it a value.
  • Using double quotes for a single character: write 'A', not "A".

Key Points

  • Every variable has a type: int, float, double or char.
  • printf uses %d, %f, %c and %s to show values.
  • scanf needs the address of the variable (&x) and %lf for double.
  • A char is a small number, so it prints as a letter with %c and as a number with %d.
  • Use const or #define for values that must not change.

Operators & Conditions

Arithmetic operators

Operators are symbols that work on values. The arithmetic operators are + - * / %. The most surprising one for beginners is /. When both numbers are int, C throws away the decimal part, so 17 / 5 is 3, not 3.4. The % operator gives the remainder, so 17 % 5 is 2. To get a decimal answer, make at least one side a double, for example with a cast like (double)a / b.

Shortcuts save typing: x += 10 means x = x + 10, and x++ adds one.

blocks.output:
a + b = 22
a - b = 12
a * b = 85
a / b = 3
a % b = 2
real division = 3.40
x = 16

blocks.html:
To print a percent sign with printf, write %%.

Comparison and logical operators

Comparison operators ask a question about two values: == (equal), != (not equal), <, >, <=, >=. In C there is no separate true/false type in older code. A comparison gives 1 for true and 0 for false, and any non-zero value counts as true in a condition.

Logical operators join conditions: && (and), || (or) and ! (not).

OperatorMeaningExample
&&both must be truemarks >= 50 && attendance >= 75
||at least one is trueday == 6 || day == 7
!reverses true and false!(x > 3)

blocks.output:
marks > 50: 1
marks == 62: 1
both conditions: 0
either condition: 1
not: 0

blocks.html:
if / else and switch

An if statement runs a block only when its condition is true. Add else if for more choices and else for everything else. A switch compares one value with several fixed cases. Each case should end with break. Without break the program keeps running into the next case, which is called fall-through.

blocks.output:
Grade B
Wednesday

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Writing if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5). A single = assigns a value, it does not compare.
  • Expecting 7 / 2 to be 3.5. It is 3 because both numbers are integers.
  • Forgetting break in a switch case.
  • Writing 0 < x < 10. Write x > 0 && x < 10 instead.

Key Points

  • Integer division drops the decimals; % gives the remainder.
  • Comparisons give 1 (true) or 0 (false); any non-zero value is true.
  • &&, || and ! combine conditions.
  • Use == to compare and = to assign.
  • Use break at the end of each switch case.

Loops

Why loops?

A loop repeats a block of code. Without loops you would have to copy the same line again and again. C has three loops: for, while and do-while. All of them check a condition to decide whether to run the block one more time.

LoopUse it whenCondition checked
foryou know how many times to repeatbefore each round
whileyou repeat until something changesbefore each round
do-whilethe block must run at least onceafter each round

The for loop

A for loop has three parts in the brackets: a start, a condition, and an update. For example, for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) starts with i = 1, continues while i is at most 5, and adds 1 after every round. Declaring int i inside the loop works in C99 and later.

while and do-while

A while loop checks the condition first, so it may run zero times. A do-while loop runs the block first and checks afterwards, so it always runs at least once. Make sure something inside the loop changes the condition, or the loop will never stop.

blocks.output:
100 50 25 12 6 3 
do-while ran with k = 10

blocks.html:
break and continue

break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one. In a for loop, the update part still runs after continue.

Common mistakes

  • A semicolon right after the brackets, like for (...);, which makes the loop body empty.
  • Forgetting to update the variable in a while loop, which creates an infinite loop.
  • Off-by-one errors: i < 5 runs 5 times from 0, but i <= 5 runs 6 times.
  • Using = instead of == in the loop condition.

Key Points

  • for is best when the number of rounds is known.
  • while checks first; do-while runs at least once.
  • break ends the loop; continue skips to the next round.
  • Always make sure the loop condition can become false.

Functions

What is a function?

A function is a named block of code that does one job. You write it once and call it many times. Functions make programs shorter, easier to read and easier to test. You have already used two: main and printf.

A function definition has a return type, a name, a list of parameters, and a body:

int square(int n) {
    return n * n;
}

The word int before the name is the return type. Use void if the function returns nothing. The return statement sends a value back to the caller and ends the function.

Prototypes

C reads your file from top to bottom. If you call a function before the compiler has seen it, you get an error or a warning. A prototype is a one-line promise placed near the top, such as int square(int n);. It tells the compiler the name, parameters and return type. The full definition can then come later, usually after main.

Pass by value

When you call a function, C copies each argument into the parameter. This is called pass by value. The function works on its own copy, so changing the parameter does not change the variable in the caller.

blocks.output:
inside the function: x = 99
back in main: a = 3

blocks.html:
The variable a stays 3. If a function needs to change the caller's variable, you pass its address. You will learn how in the pointers lesson. A function can return only one value directly, so use the return value for the result.

A realistic example

This function calculates an average from three marks. Notice that it divides by 3.0 (a double), so the result keeps its decimals.

blocks.output: Average = 81.00

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Calling a function before its prototype or definition.
  • Forgetting return in a function that must return a value.
  • Expecting a function to change the caller's variable. Parameters are copies.
  • Passing the wrong number of arguments or the wrong types.

Key Points

  • A function has a return type, a name, parameters and a body.
  • A prototype declares a function so it can be called before it is defined.
  • C passes arguments by value, so the function gets copies.
  • return sends one value back; void means nothing is returned.

Arrays & Strings

Arrays

An array stores many values of the same type in one row of memory. You write the size in square brackets: int marks[5];. Items are numbered from 0, so the first item is marks[0] and the last one in a size-5 array is marks[4]. C does not check the index. If you use marks[5], you read memory that does not belong to the array, and the program may crash or give garbage.

You can give starting values with braces: int marks[5] = {70, 85, 60, 92, 78};. A loop is the natural way to visit every item.

blocks.output:
marks[0] = 70
marks[1] = 85
marks[2] = 60
marks[3] = 92
marks[4] = 78
Sum = 385
Average = 77.0

blocks.html:
Strings are char arrays

C has no separate string type. A string is an array of char that ends with a special character called the null terminator, written '\0' (its value is 0). Functions such as printf use it to know where the text stops. So the string "Ali" needs 4 bytes: 'A', 'l', 'i' and '\0'.

blocks.output:
Text: Ali
Array size: 4
Length: 3
name[0] = 65
name[1] = 108
name[2] = 105
name[3] = 0

blocks.html:
The array size is 4, but strlen counts only the visible characters, so it says 3. The last item, name[3], is 0, the terminator.

Useful functions from string.h

Add #include <string.h> to use these helpers. You cannot copy or compare strings with = and ==, because those would work on addresses, not on the letters.

FunctionWhat it does
strlen(s)number of characters before the '\0'
strcpy(dest, src)copies src into dest
strcat(dest, src)adds src to the end of dest
strcmp(a, b)0 if equal, negative if a comes first, positive if b comes first

blocks.output:
full = Sara Khan
length = 9
same? 1
apple before banana? 1

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Using index equal to the size, such as a[5] in a size-5 array.
  • Making a char array too small. char s[3] = "Ali"; leaves no room for '\0'.
  • Comparing strings with ==. Use strcmp.
  • Copying into a buffer that is too small with strcpy or strcat.

Key Points

  • Array indexes start at 0 and C does not check bounds.
  • A string is a char array that ends with '\0', so it needs one extra byte.
  • strlen does not count the terminator; sizeof of the array does.
  • Use strcpy, strcat and strcmp from string.h.

Pointers

Memory has addresses

Every variable lives somewhere in memory, and every location has an address. A pointer is a variable that stores an address. Pointers look scary at first, but they are just a way to say "the value lives over there". They let functions change the caller's data, and they are the base of arrays, strings and dynamic memory in C.

SyntaxMeaning
int *p;p is a pointer to an int
&xaddress-of: the address of x
*pdereference: the value p points to

Address-of and dereference

Write int *p = &x; to make p point to x. Then *p means "the thing at that address", so reading or writing *p is the same as reading or writing x.

blocks.output:
x = 10, *p = 10
x = 25
p points to x? 1

blocks.html:
Pointers and arrays

The name of an array is converted to the address of its first item. So int *p = a; makes p point to a[0]. Adding 1 to a pointer moves it to the next item (not the next byte), so *(p + 1) is the same as a[1]. Also p[2] is allowed and means *(p + 2).

Pass by pointer

Remember that C passes copies of arguments. If you pass the address of a variable, the function receives a copy of the address, and it can use * to reach the original variable. This is how scanf can fill your variables.

blocks.output:
after swap_copy: x=4 y=9
after swap: x=9 y=4

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Using a pointer that was never set. An uninitialised pointer points to a random place. Set it to an address or to NULL.
  • Dereferencing NULL, which crashes the program.
  • Mixing up p (the address) and *p (the value).
  • Walking past the end of an array with a pointer.

Key Points

  • A pointer stores the address of another variable.
  • &x gets an address; *p reaches the value at an address.
  • An array name works like a pointer to its first item; p + 1 moves to the next item.
  • Pass a pointer to let a function change the caller's variable.

Structs, Memory & Files

Structs and typedef

An array holds many values of the same type. A struct groups values of different types under one name, such as a student with a name, a roll number and a GPA. Each part is called a member, and you reach it with a dot: s.roll. With typedef you give the struct a short type name so you do not need to write struct every time.

If you have a pointer to a struct, use the arrow ->: sp->roll is the same as (*sp).roll. Assigning one struct to another copies all its members.

blocks.output:
Ayesha (roll 12) GPA 3.6
Ayesha (roll 12) GPA 3.6
Bilal (roll 13) GPA 3.6

blocks.html:
malloc and free

Normal variables have a fixed size decided when you write the code. Sometimes you only know the size while the program runs. malloc(bytes) from stdlib.h asks the system for that much memory and returns a pointer to it, or NULL if it fails. When you are done, give the memory back with free. If you forget, the program has a memory leak.

blocks.output: Sum = 150

blocks.html:
Reading and writing text files

To use a file, call fopen(name, mode). It returns a FILE *, or NULL if it fails. Common modes are "w" (write, creates or empties the file), "a" (append) and "r" (read). Then use fprintf to write text like printf, and fgets to read one line. Always finish with fclose.

FunctionJob
fopenopen a file, check for NULL
fprintf(f, ...)write formatted text to the file
fgets(buf, size, f)read one line into buf, returns NULL at the end
fclose(f)close the file and save the data

blocks.output:
Read: Ali 75
Read: Sara 88

blocks.html:
The line from fgets still contains the newline character, so the demo prints it without adding another \n.

Common mistakes

  • Not checking if malloc or fopen returned NULL.
  • Forgetting free (a leak) or using memory after it was freed.
  • Calling malloc(n) for ints. Multiply by the type size: n * sizeof(int).
  • Forgetting fclose, so data may not be saved.
  • Using . with a pointer to a struct. Use ->.

Key Points

  • A struct groups different types; typedef gives it a short name.
  • Use . on a struct and -> on a pointer to a struct.
  • malloc reserves memory at run time and free releases it.
  • fopen, fprintf, fgets and fclose handle text files.
  • Always check for NULL after malloc and fopen.
